Research done with WebSearch/WebFetch on 2026-10-17. What happened: the 10-14 to 10-16 selloff was macro and positioning, not a demand break. September CPI (released 10-14) printed 3.7% headline / 2.6% core vs 3.6% / 2.5% expected, gasoline +9.1% m/m, pushing December Fed-hike odds to ~94% (Citi now calls a December hike; October 27-28 meeting odds ~15-32%). The same day a chart of CoreWeave's 2031/2032 bond yields (~15-16%, CDS >1,100bp, ~$50B debt) went viral and the 'AI debt' scare hit the whole capex chain: CRWV -16%, AMD -5.7% on 10-14, SOXX down nine straight sessions (longest streak since 2006), Nasdaq -4.5% on the week, VIX to 22. Brent touched $110 on Iran's escalating Hormuz attacks. 10-year ~5.07-5.10% and 30-year ~5.42%, both retreating from the 10-07 peak (30-year fell 10bp on 10-16). What did NOT happen: fundamentals did not break. TSMC reported on 10-15 a record quarter (revenue ~$46.7B above the top of guidance, net income +69% y/y, Q4 guided $52.3-54.3B = +14% q/q, 2026 capex reiterated $60-64B, 2026-28 capex 'significantly higher') and TSM still fell and stopped out of this book at 412.61 on 10-16 - that is a sell-everything tape, not a verdict on foundry demand. Micron's FQ4 beat ($33.42 EPS on $54.2B vs $31.61/$51.1B est.) with a guide above consensus and trades near ~7x forward at ~$880; its 5-day 16% slide was tied to rates and a CXMT China DRAM report, and a buyback restriction lifts 12-09. ASML said it may not be able to meet 2027 demand. BofA argues the AI trade is resilient on GPU utilization; Nvidia's CEO publicly backed CoreWeave. Why trade rather than hold: my 10-05 stops now sit 0.6% (ANET), 2% (AMD) and 3% (MU) away on names that move 4-8% a day. Holding would almost certainly mean getting stopped out at the low of a record losing streak and then sitting in 56%+ cash through any relief bounce, which is the worst of both worlds. Either I believe the mandate or I do not; I do, so I re-base stops to Monday's fill. Why lower gross: the macro genuinely changed since 10-05 - a hike cycle resuming with Brent at $110 is a stagflationary backdrop that compresses high-multiple semis regardless of earnings - so I cut gross from 78% (68% after the TSM stop) to 63%, trim MU from 24% to 16% (highest beta, China-competition overhang, 24% was too much single-name risk), trim AMD 14% to 10%, and re-add TSM at 8% after its record print at a ~15% discount to two weeks ago. NVDA stays at 16% as the highest-quality, least-drawn-down core leg; ANET trims to 8%. BTC stays at 5% unchanged (stop unchanged) as the small contrarian leg - it is in a downtrend (36% off its high, ETF outflows, ~$1B of longs liquidated on the CPI day) but the mandate sized it small for exactly that, and churning it costs 35bps each way. 37% cash at 4% is dry powder for the 10-27/28 Fed decision and the 10-29 PCE print. Known risks I accept: a December hike is now consensus and the Fed could surprise in October; CoreWeave's debt could become a real credit event; oil could spike further. Stops are set to survive one more bad week but not a regime break.

Cash is the hedge against the fuel-crisis premium deflating on a Hormuz deal. It replaces the airline leg, which lost money on both sides of that trade.
book.reassessment_note: The airline leg was supposed to be the other side of the crack spread: management-quantified fuel relief that would pay if a Hormuz deal deflated fuel prices. No deal arrived. Crude kept rising (USO 143.99 -> 161.76 from 10-05 to 10-16, BNO 61.45 -> 67.19), and the airlines fell faster than the refiners rose (JETS -7.3%, UAL -12.6%, DAL 83.08 -> 75.37). Delta's 10-09 report changed the picture. It cut full-year adjusted EPS to $5.10-5.60 from $6.50-7.50, guided Q4 margins of 7-9% on about $4.25/gal all-in fuel, and said Q3 absorbed more than $500M of fuel cost above its July plan. United's Q3 guide was built on $3.69/gal from the July 14 curve, so the 'quantified relief' premise has failed. United reports on 10-20 after the close, the day after this entry, so holding it means a binary print with the stock 5.5% above an 18% stop. I am closing both airline legs. The deal-deflation hedge they were meant to provide now comes from cash at 4% APY, which does not bleed when crude rises. The refiners keep their weights. Research I could do: web search found the EIA expecting US diesel cracks above $2/gal through November, Gulf refineries still offline with recovery seen only into 2027, and talk of a US diesel export ban in late September. Search found no October-dated Hormuz coverage, so I cannot rule out a deal. That is why I am not adding refiner weight after a +6-10% two-week run, and why the stops are tightened to 10% from the new fill. Prices are Yahoo daily closes through 10-16.

positions.thesis: MPC is the largest of the three because it has the biggest US refining footprint and its mid-continent and Gulf Coast crude advantage. It has led the move: 433.47 -> 478.07 since 10-05, with 10-14 the new high at 484.92. The EIA expects diesel cracks above $2/gal through November, and Gulf product exports are still impaired. Q3 earnings in late October/early November should show the record August-September cracks (the ULSD crack peaked at $102/bbl on 8-17). The 10% stop from the new fill locks in most of the gain if a Hormuz products deal finally lands.

PSX is the lowest-crack-beta refiner here: midstream, chemicals and marketing dampen it both ways. That makes it the right mid-sized leg when crack exposure is wanted but a deal headline could gap the pure refiners. It is up 269.72 -> 293.17 since 10-05 and held up better than VLO on the 10-15 pullback (-2.7% vs -3.4%). It keeps the same weight. The 10% stop runs from the new fill.

VLO is the highest-crack-beta, most export-exposed of the three (Gulf Coast distillate to Europe and Latin America), so it is the smallest leg. It has the most upside if diesel stays scarce and the most downside if a US diesel export ban or a Hormuz products reopening hits Gulf Coast export margins. It reports Q3 first of the three, around 10-22, which gives an early read on how much of the record crack was captured. It is up 419.33 -> 444.71 since 10-05 and slipped back from the 10-14 high of 459.78, which is another reason not to size it up. The 10% stop runs from the new fill.

Risks accepted: the AI-credit contagion widens and the sleeve stops out (cost roughly 1-2% of NAV beyond current marks); JNJ's Q3 talc charge and soft MedTech are known and the stock has already recovered above my fill.
